title: 1.e4 Part 1: The Vienna
description: In Part 1, we focus on 1.e4 e5 by Black, and Levy's main recommendation: the wonderful Vienna. Pair this course with the "Dark Vienna" to really skyrocket your Vienna power.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4B3/3q4/2N5/PPP1Q1PP/.text:
Success! 

We capture Black's e-pawn and Black is going to lose everything.

r1b1kbnr/ppppqppp/2n5/4P3/3P1p2/2N2N2/PP.text:
We continue with 7.d4 and the threat of Nd5 is borderline unstoppable. 

White has a winning advantage.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/3P1B2/2N2N2/PPP.text:
We continue with 8.Qe2.

We know this position. 8...Nxd4 9.Nxd4 and we will play Bxe5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/3P1p2/2N2N2/PPP.text:
7...Nc6 is the most popular response at this point, but Black can do other things (we will review briefly in the video).

We take on f4 with the bishop. This is the important move, taking advantage of the pin. We also set up traps.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4P3/3P1p2/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black undermines your pawn, and prepares to develop their light-squared Bishop.

We capture Black's f4-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3n1B2/2N2N2/PPP1Q.text:
Black takes, threatening your queen.

We trade knights.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/5p2/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Black can also continue with 5...Nc6, a more flexible move.

We continue with d4 - expanding in the center and supporting the e-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/5n2/4P3/5p2/2N5/PPPP2P.text:
Black plays 4...Qe7 and pins the e-pawn.

We continue by unpinning the pawn with 5.Qe2 - mirroring Black's move.

Now, Black has no choice - the knight must depart.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1qppp/3p4/4P3/5p2/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Black plays 6...d6 to develop the light-squared Bishop.

Let's play the knockout punch, punishing the queen for standing in front of the King.

rnb1kbnr/ppppqppp/8/4P3/5p2/2N5/PPPPQ1PP.text:
Black's knight retreats. Black is now threatening Qh4+.

We now develop and cover the check.

rnb1kbnr/pppq1ppp/3P4/3N4/5p2/5N2/PPPPQ1.text: We chop down Black's position and win the game.

rnb1kbnr/pppq1ppp/3p4/3NP3/5p2/5N2/PPPPQ.text: Black's queen slides to safety, but...

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
In this chapter, Black replies with 2...Nf6, allowing us to push 3.f4 next - the Vienna Gambit!

We offer Black a capture of our f-pawn in order to push 4.e5 and attack the enemy knight...

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/4Pp2/2N5/PPPP2PP.text:
You will face this a shocking amount of times. 
It simply lands Black in a dead lost position on move 3! 

This is our plan: 
4.e5
5.Nf3 
6.d4 
Finally, aim to capture the pawn back.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/5p2/2N2N2/PPPP2.text:
Black undermines your pawn, and prepares to develop his light-squared bishop.

We continue with 6.d4. 

If Black captures in the center afterwards, our queen will become active.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3P1p2/2N2N2/PPP3P.text:
Black captures the e-pawn.

We continue with 7.Qe2 - this is very important! 

Now Black is frozen, you avoid a trade of queens, and you will recapture both center pawns before castling - preferably queenside.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/5p2/2N5/PPPP2PP/.text:
Black decides to retreat the knight - this is the only safe square. 

Black is now threatening Qh4+.

You MUST play Nf3 before you push d4, as this prevents Black's Qh4+.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image 1...e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight.

This is slightly different than 2.Nf3, which is standard development.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first study of the Vienna! 

This study will introduce the so-called Vienna Gambit and answer the question: after 
1.e4 e5 
2.Nc3 Nf6 
3.f4
What if Black simply takes our f-pawn?

White gets a fun and easy game!

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/2n2n2/4P3/3P4/2N5/PPP1.text:
Instead, we should simply respond with 7.Be2. 

This unpins our e-pawn, and keeps our queen watching our d-pawn.

A reasonable move after this would be something like Nf3, defending the center.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/2n2n2/4P3/3P4/2N5/PPP3.text:
A tricky response for Black would be to pin our e-pawn with 6... Qe7. 

If we mirror the move with 7. Qe2 then Black can respond with 7... Nxd4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4PP2/2N5/PPP.text:
Believe it or not, defending the Vienna Gambit with 3...Nc6 is one of Black's most popular responses.

But, fortunately for us, this puts Black in a losing position!

You must take after Black plays 3...Nc6.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
Of course, Black can go back this way too, but it's not quite effective.

We push 6.e5, advancing and attacking the knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4n3/4P3/2N5/PPPP2P.text:
Black recaptures on e5.

You have to push d4 to target the knights.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5nn1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP3PP.text:
This is 1 of 2 retreats available for Black.

Of the 2, this one is the better option for Black.

We push 6.e5 and attack Black's knight! 

Black must retreat with ...Ng8 now.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B2p3/3P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black captures the e-pawn.

We recapture with the knight, pressuring the c6-knight.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4P3/3P4/2N2N2/PPP3.text:
Black undermines the e-pawn, and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

We continue by pinning Black's knight with 8.Bb5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p2n1/4P3/3P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
7...d6 is Black's most direct attempt at fighting back against the center.

We don't need to be afraid - we develop the light-squared bishop and target Black's king.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/6n1/4p3/2BP4/2N2N2/PPP3.text:
Black captures the e-pawn.

We simply castle.  

We now have the entire kingside developed, and we're ready to strike.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/6n1/6N1/2Bp4/2N5/PPP3PP.text:
We continue with 10.Ng5.

There are unstoppable intentions on f7. White is completely winning!

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/6n1/8/2Bp4/2N2N2/PPP3PP.text: Black is greedy and captures the d-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/3P4/2N5/PPP3PP.text:
Black retreats the knight to g8.

We again cover Qh4+ and defend the center. 7.Nf3 Bb4 8.d5 is good for us.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/6n1/4P3/3P4/2N5/PPP3PP.text:
Black retreats the knight to g8.

Nf3 is a flexible developing move and it prevents an annoying Qh4+.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/2n5/1B2N3/3P4/2N5/PPP3P.text:
Black supports the c6-knight with 9...Bd7.

We will capture the bishop with 10.Nxd7.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/2n5/1B1P4/8/2N5/PPP3PP/R.text:
We continue with 11.d5, creating tactics in our favor.

11...Qe7+ 12.Qe2 a6 13.dxc6 and White comes out on top because we can take on b7 at the end of many variations.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/2n5/1B6/3P4/2N5/PPP3PP/R.text:
Black recaptures on d7 and is ready to castle queenside.

Let's make sure they don't get the time.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text: In this chapter, Black replies with 2...Nf6, allowing us to push 3.f4 next - the Vienna Gambit!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image 1...e5, the most popular reply at all levels. 

We develop our queenside knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're continuing our analysis of the Vienna Gambit and taking a look at how to respond if Black declines our gambit with 3...Nc6.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/4PP2/2N2N2/P.text:
Black develops with 4...Nc6, supporting the center - this is most common.

We will pin the c6 knight to make the e-pawn a target.

r2q1rk1/p1p1bppp/2p2n2/4p3/4P3/2NP1Q1P/P.text:
We continue 11.d3, with a pleasant position. 

We will develop the dark-squared bishop and attempt to target Black's weaknesses.

If Black activates their rook with ...Rb8, don't play b3! 

Instead, we can support the pawn with Nd1 or Rb1.

r2qk2r/p1p1bppp/2p2n2/4p3/4P3/2N2Q1P/PPP.text:
Black recaptures and now their pawn structure is in ruins. 

We shall castle, push d3, and have a calm advantage.

r2qk2r/p1p1bppp/2pp1n2/4p3/4PP2/2N2Q1P/P.text:
Black recaptures on c6.

We capture on e5.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4PP2/2N2Q1P.text:
Black develops with 7...Be7 and prepares O-O. 

I recommend a very simple transformation of the position.

We capture on c6 - giving up the bishop pair, but ruining Black's pawn structure.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4PP2/2N2Q1P.text: Our main objectives are to undermine e5. We will take on c6 and double the pawns, and then open up the f-file.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4PP2/2N2b1P.text:
Black captures on f3.

We recapture with the queen.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4PPb1/2N2N2.text:
Sometimes, this pin occurs.

We should attack the bishop with 6.h3.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/4PP2/2N2Q1P/P.text:
Black develops with 6...Nc6, supporting the center.

We continue with 7.Bb5.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4PP2/2N2N2.text:
Black unpins the knight with 5...Bd7.

We continue with 6.d3. 

Now we are ready to capture on c6, followed by e5.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2np1n2/1B6/4PB2/2NP1N2/.text:
We recapture with the bishop.

Our position is very comfortable and we will continue with Qd2 or Qe2, followed by castling kingside or queenside.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2np1n2/1B6/4Pp2/2NP1N2/.text: Black releases the tension and captures on f4.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/3p1n2/1B2p3/3nPP2/2NP1N.text:
Black also has the option to jump the knight onto d4. The following line is pretty forced.

We capture the bishop on d7 with check.

r3kb1r/pp1q1ppp/3p1n2/2p5/3pPP2/3P4/PPP1.text:
We castle our king. 

We have a pretty comfortable position. If Black castles kingside some of our ideas include Ng3, Bd2 and f5.

If Black castles queenside, some of our attacking ideas include a4 + b4 + Rb1, but we can also attack Black's center with c3.

r3kb1r/pppq1ppp/3p1n2/4p3/3nPP2/2NP1N2/P.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

We capture the knight on d4.

r3kb1r/pppq1ppp/3p1n2/8/3pPP2/2NP4/PPP3P.text:
Black recaptures on d4 and attacks our knight.

We retreat our knight to e2 and attack the d-pawn.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/4p3/4PP2/2N2Q1P/P.text: If Black opts to develop with 6...Be7, we can continue developing with Bc4 + O-O + d3.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p2b/4PP2/2N2N1P/.text: If Black retreats the bishop to h5, we can trap it with g4 + f5.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/4PP2/2N2b1P/P.text:
Black captures on f3.

We recapture with the queen.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/4PPb1/2N2N2/P.text:
Black can also pin our knight with 4...Bg4 - this is actually the second most common move.

We immediately attack the bishop with 5.h3.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/4Pp2/2N2Q1P/PPP.text:
If Black takes on f4, we can play d4!

Bxf4 will follow, and White has a position with total central control. 0-0 will also add a rook to the semi-open f-file.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p1n2/8/3PPp2/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black plays 5...Qe7 - counterattacking our center. 

Don't rush, respect the opponent's threats.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p1n2/8/3PPp2/2NB1N2/P.text:
We defend the e-pawn with 6.Bd3. 

White is better, and we will simply continue by capturing on f4.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2p1p/3p1N2/7q/3PPp2/8/PPP3PP.text:
We continue with 9.Nf6+, forking Black's king and queen! 

Black's king is now forced to move. Soon we will capture the queen and win the f4-pawn.

Black's position is terrible and White has a winning advantage.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2p1p/3p4/3N2qn/3PPp2/8/PPP3P.text:
Black captures on g5.

We can capture Black's knight on h5, temporarily sacrificing our queen!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/3p4/3N2pn/3PPp2/5N2/PPP.text:
Black defends the f-pawn with 6...g5, but this is a mistake!

We sacrifice the knight on g5!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/4PP2/2N5/PPPP.text:
Declining with 3...d6 is extremely common.

We will simply develop our knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/4Pp2/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Black captures on f4, but there is nothing to worry about here.

We continue with 5.d4 - grabbing central space and opening up an attack on Black's f4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/7n/3PPp2/2N2N2/PPP3.text:
Black can also try to defend the pawn with 5...Nh5.

We respond 6.Nd5 - attacking the f4 pawn once more.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text: In this chapter, Black replies with 2...Nf6, allowing us to push 3.f4 next - the Vienna Gambit!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image 1...e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're continuing our analysis of the Vienna Gambit and taking a look at how to respond if Black declines our gambit with 3...d6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2B1PP2/2NP1.text:
Black defends.

And here we can go f5!

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/4pPB1/2P1P3/2N2N.text: We recapture. We're going to bring our queen up and castle queenside to attack on the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/n3pP2/2B1P3/2NP1.text:
Black usually goes for the bishop, as they should. 

If they don't do this, feel free to preserve your bishop with a3 ideas.

And here I suggest we develop the other bishop.

r2q1k1r/p1p1b1pp/2pp4/5b2/3N4/8/PPP2PPP/.text: The knight jumps into the center of the board! White is winning.

r2q1k1r/ppp1b1pp/2np4/3B1b2/3p4/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black is advised to break the pin because Bg5 was coming!

Let's remove d4's defender.

r2qk2r/ppp1b1pp/2np1n2/5b2/2Bp4/2N2N2/PP.text: If the bishop blocks, Nd5 adds an attacker...

r2qk2r/ppp1b1pp/2np4/3n1b2/2Bp4/5N2/PPP2.text: Black is compelled to take, and logically we recapture.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/4pb2/2B5/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black develops the knight, and so here comes d4! 

This is actually very strong: if massive exchanges occur on e5, Black would have an isolated pawn!

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/5b2/2Bp4/2N2N2/PPP.text: Just to exemplify how badly things can go, we can give a check here.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/7b/2B1PB2/2NP1N1.text: The bishop goes back, so we attack it once more.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/2B1PBb1/2NP1N2.text: If Black goes for this very popular move, just kick them out with h3. If Bxf3, Qxf3, and you have the bishop pair.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1nb1/8/2B1PBP1/2NP1N.text:
It goes back.

We now develop the queen.
Now, in this particular position, 0-0-0 is more logical! The attack has been set up on the kingside!

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/4pb2/2B5/2N2N2/PPP.text: Thus after Black develops, we simply continue with our plan of 0-0.

rn1qkbnr/ppp3pp/3p4/4pb2/2B5/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
Black here usually recaptures.

But now we have a plan: Nf3, 0-0 and d4!

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/4p3/2B1PP2/2NP4/.text:
Sometimes, Black just castles.

Let's add pressure on e5 with our knight.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/2B1PB2/2NP4/PP.text:
Black castles.

And now we continue developing our pieces, getting ready to castle.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/5n2/8/3pNB2/1B1P4/PPP1Q1.text: We can get our knight out of danger and castle afterwards.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/4p3/2B1P3/2NP4/PP.text:
Black usually continues with normal development.

Let's play f4!

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/2B1Pp2/2NP4/PPP.text:
It's not unusual for Black to take.

We just recapture, that's why our bishop is there!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/3p4/2B1PB2/2NP4/PP.text: ...d5 is achieved, but we can simply trade.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2pp1n2/4p3/2B1P3/2NP4/PP.text:
The knight is brought out to support d5.

We push.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2pp1n2/8/2B1Pp2/2NP4/PPP.text:
Black resolves the tension before pushing d5.

We recapture.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/3p4/2B2B2/2NP4/PPP3P.text:
Black takes.

Let's bring the bishop to b3.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/8/3p1B2/1BNP4/PPP3PP.text: And if d4, we first insert a check.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PPP.text:
This is the most popular move. Black develops a knight.

4.d3 protects the e4 pawn and opens up the dark-squared bishop. 

5.f4 will be our next move.

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/2pp4/pp2p3/4P3/1BNP4/PPP2P.text: And if they threaten to trap your bishop...

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/2pp4/pp2p3/P3P3/1BNP4/1PP2.text:
Just don't let that happen!

Our idea is to play f4 and Nf3. If 6...b4 7.Nce2 is solid for White.

rnbqkbnr/p4ppp/2pp4/1p2p3/2B1P3/2NP4/PPP.text: If Black goes for b5 ideas, we bring the bishop backwards.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2pp4/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PPPP1.text:
For some reason, this move is the second most popular on the lichess player database.

d3 and f4 is our plan. Without a knight on c6, Black is less equipped to deal with pressure on e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
This is definitely a passive setup, but it's completely possible.

We develop the bishop first, before going for the d3/f4 setup.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/3p4/4pp2/2B1P3/2N5/PPPP1.text:
Some players are crazy like this! 

They go for ...f5 to undermine the center.

Let's just take. Did Black really think this through?

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black will mirror us.

We'll play Nc3, starting up our Vienna. 

And now this is where Black will deviate. 2...Bc5, Bb4 or d6!

As 2...d6 is our subject, we'll see that in this study.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We have to study what can happen if Black deviates from theory on move 2! 

We will begin with the move 2...d6, a slow pawn move that could be played.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n2n2/8/4P3/2Q1BP2/PPP3.text:
Just castle queenside, and you'll stand much better. 

Even if Black does find the idea of trading queens, we can just go ahead and trade and develop our bishops which control many squares.
So suppose they play Nc6 which is a developing move...

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp4/2b1pP2/3nP3/1B1P1N2.text:
In which case we should just retreat. 

In case of ...a5, we've got Nxd4 and a4, followed by Qf3 to develop our queen.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp4/2bBpP2/3nP3/3P1N2/P.text: Black usually pushes the pawn to dislodge our bishop...

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/1b1p4/4pPB1/2BnP1n1/2NP.text:
You can keep all the threats alive by moving the queen away. 

White has a winning position.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/1bnp4/4pP2/2B1P1n1/2NP1.text:
If 9...Nc6, 10.Bg5 is also great for White.

We will play Bg5 because Black has a problem on the kingside. They lack defenders.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/2B1PP2/2NP.text:
6...Nc6 is a close second in terms of popularity.

I suggest we prioritize kingside play with f5.

Bg5 is a strong idea.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/2b1pP2/2BnP3/2NP1.text:
Black's best move is ...Nd4.

We should put our knight on d5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p4/2bnpP2/2BnP3/3P1N2/.text: If Black takes, we've got to keep the integrity of our structure by recapturing with the bishop.

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/1pnp4/4p3/4PP2/5N2/PPPP.text:
Black recaptures.

2kr1b1r/pppq2pp/2n1b3/4Pp2/2Pp4/3P1BQ1/P.text:
We move our bishop to f3. With the opposite side castling, the position is incredibly dynamic and there are attacking prospects for both sides.
Before trying to launch any sort of attack, we should look to finish our development with Ne2 and O-O.

Any h7-h6 (looking to expand with g5) should simply be met with h2-h4.

2kr1b1r/pppq2pp/2n1b3/4Pp2/2Pp4/3P2Q1/P1.text: Black castles queenside and defends the b7-pawn with their king.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n5/4Pp2/3p4/2PP2Q1/P1P3.text:
Black continues normal development - further increasing their central control.

Another important moment: we must develop Be2 before moving our knight, as we threaten Bh5+ here.

r2q1rk1/ppp3pp/2n1b3/4Pp2/1bPp4/3P2QN/P1.text:
We move our knight to h3. This move keeps the f3 square available for our light-squared bishop, and allows us to put our bishop/knight on g5. 

The computer gives equality, but White is very active and has good attacking prospects on the kingside. 

We can continue developing with Bg5/Ng5, Bf3 and Rb1.

r2qk2r/ppp3pp/2n1b3/4Pp2/1bPp4/3P2Q1/P1P.text:
Black makes use of the newly opened e1-a5 diagonal by moving their bishop to b4 and giving a check to our king.

d1 is safe for it.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2n1b3/4Pp2/3p4/2PP2Q1/P1P.text:
Black develops the bishop to e6.

This move also defends against the threat of Bh5+ as ...g6 is now a viable option since Bxg6+ can simply be met with ...hxg6 Qxg6+ Bf7.

We will control d5 by pushing c4.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/4b3/4Pp2/1nPp4/3P2Q1/P1P1.text: Black jumps the knight into b4 and threatens to capture on c2.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/4b3/4Pp2/1nPp4/3P2Q1/P1P3.text:
We defend the c2-pawn by retreating our bishop back to d1. 

The position is somewhat complicated, but White has an edge and White's position is easier to play - We will look to continue with Nh3 & O-O, and can at any point kick out Black's knight with a2-a3.

r3kb1r/pppq2pp/2n1b3/4Pp2/2Pp4/3P2Q1/P1P.text:
Black moves the queen up to d7 and prepares to castle queenside.

We respond by moving our rook to b1 and attacking Black's b7-pawn.

If Black ever gives a check with their bishop, we can move the king to d1, where it will be safe.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/8/3pPp2/4n3/2N2Q2/PPPP2P.text:
I'll be very clear: this is the best move in my experience, but we will try to mix things up here regardless. By playing ...f5 Black has made a similar commitment that White made on move 3 - increasing their control of the center, but weakening the diagonal leading to their king.

Let's attack the knight with d3.

This is the critical response - Black is "physically" preventing us from getting a solid central structure with c3-d4-e5. Now, it is important that we don't just capture this pawn as after ...Qxd4, both our rook and e5 pawn would be under attack.

Let's move the queen to a more active square.

We recapture on d5. Temporarily down a pawn, but with an advantage in development and sufficient dynamic compensation.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/8/2pqnp2/3p4/2PP2P1/P1P1N.text: Black trades the queens - there isn't really a better option since the e5 knight was attacked by White's queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/2n5/2p1Pp2/3p4/2PP1QP1/P1.text:
This somewhat counter-intuitive move is actually the critical response to ...Bg2. For the cost of the opening of the long diagonal, Black is successfully preventing us from getting a solid central structure with c3-d4-e5.

Let's develop our knight, as development is more important than the e5-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/2n5/2ppPp2/8/2PP1QP1/P1P4.text:
Black simply continues by developing their knight, putting some pressure on the e5-pawn.

We can ignore the attack and continue with our plan of Bg2, since ...Nxe5 can be met with Qe2 + d4. Black's d5-pawn would also be weak in many lines.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/8/2p1np2/3p4/2PP1QP1/P1P1.text:
In this instance, Black does capture the undefended e5-pawn, as White no longer has the idea of Qe2 + d4.

This is an important move - we should absolutely offer the queen trade on d5.

r2qkb1r/pp4pp/2n1b3/2ppPp2/8/2PP1QP1/P1P.text:
Black continues developing naturally and supports the d5 pawn.

Nh3 is an important move! We want to bring the knight to g5, from where it will be exerting a great amount of pressure on Black's position.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2n1b3/3pPp2/8/2PP1Q2/P1P1.text:
This is probably most natural. Black develops the knight, attacking our e5 pawn and supporting the center.

We can actually ignore the attack on the pawn and instead gain a tempo on Black's undefended e6 bishop.

r3kb1r/pp1q2pp/2n1b3/2ppPp2/8/2PP1QPN/P1.text: Black develops the queen and prepares O-O-O.

r3kb1r/pp1q2pp/2n1b3/2ppPpN1/8/2PP1QP1/P.text: Our position is now amazing. The g5 knight is great and can capture the e6 bishop at any point - destabilizing Black's center. We are putting a large amount of pressure on the d5 pawn and can keep developing with O-O + Rb1.

r3kb1r/pppq2pp/2n1b3/3pPp2/3P1N2/2P2Q2/P.text: We play d4 - defending our e5 pawn and establishing a very solid central structure. White's position is now very pleasant and we will continue to develop naturally with Bd3 + O-O + Rb1.

r3kb1r/pppq2pp/2n1b3/3pPp2/5N2/2PP1Q2/P1.text:
Black defends the bishop and prepares O-O-O.

9...Nxe5 runs into 10.Qe2.

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/4b3/3pPp2/8/2PP1Q2/P1P3P.text:
This is another natural developing move and is about as common as ...Be7. Again, Black didn't play the critical ...d4 so we should be able to obtain a pleasant position.

We simply develop our knight to e2 - the same way we did it against 7...Be7.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/8/3pPp2/8/2PP1QP1/P1P1.text: We play g3 and will fianchetto our bishop on g2. The position is quite pleasant for White, and our plan now consists of Bg2 + d4 + O-O in some order.

rnbqk2r/ppp1b1pp/8/3pPp2/8/2PP1Q2/P1P3PP.text:
Black doesn't play the critical 7...d4 and develops naturally.

We simply develop our knight to e2 - from here it supports the d4 square and has access to the f4 square where it is likely to land in the future.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/8/2ppPp2/8/2PP1Q2/P1P3PP/.text:
This is inferior to the critical d5-d4, but  is a very playable move and scores quite well for Black in the database. 

By playing c7-c5, Black has increased their control over the d4 square and is intending to develop their b8 knight behind the c-pawn.

White can respond to 7...c5 in a couple of ways, but 8.g3 is a simple, yet quite an interesting idea.

And declining the Gambit is the best response for Black. However, at levels below 1600, this move is played roughly 10% of the time.

I'll be very clear: this is the best move in my experience, but we will try to mix things up here regardless. 

Black's knight on e4 is pretty annoying, so we should immediately remove it with d3.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2p1p/1bnp2p1/3Np3/2BqP1Q1/3P.text: Black plays d7-d6 and opens up an attack on our queen.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2p1p/1bnp2p1/3Np3/2BqP3/3P1Q.text: We simply slide the Queen back to f3 - out of the vision of Black's bishop. Our attacking possibilites are now endless, Black's pieces are terrible & have no harmony, and White is just completely winning.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2p1p/2np2p1/2bNp3/2BqP1Q1/3P.text: Black plays d7-d6 and opens up an attack on our queen.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2p1p/2np2p1/2bNp3/2BqP3/3P1Q.text: We simply slide the Queen back to f3 - out of the vision of Black's bishop. The threat of c2-c3 is now simply unstoppable and White is completely winning.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/1bn3p1/3Np3/2BqP1Q1/3P.text:
Noticing that their queen is getting trapped, Black attempts to free up the c5 square for their queen.

We move our rook to the semi-open file and shift our focus from trapping Black's queen to attacking Black on the king-side.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/2bNp3/2B1P1Q1/8/.text:
Black defends the g7 pawn with g7-g6. Now Nxc7+ might look really tempting, but that is not the point.

The point is Nh3! - and the queen is actually trapped.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/2bNp3/2BqP1Q1/7N.text:
Black retreats the queen to the only "free" square where it cannot be immediately captured and attacks the c4 bishop.

We defend the bishop with d2-d3 and threaten to trap Black's queen with c2-c3.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n2q2/2b1p3/2B1P1Q1/2N.text:
4...Qf6 is by far the most common, but also the worst of the three options. 

A natural move to attack and defend. But as it turns out, after ...Qf6 Black is already borderline lost!

We have the stunning idea - Nd5! 
We attack Black's queen and threaten to fork Black's king and rook with Nxc7, but we also shockingly allow Black to capture on f2.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bNp3/2B1P1Q1/8/PP.text:
Black is pretty much forced to make this capture as every other move loses material - either to Nxc7+ or Qxg7.

We slide our king over to d1, the only legal move. Now, our king is in no real danger, and we have multiple threats: Qxg7, Nxc7+ and even Nh3!

Black will try to defend in two ways: 6...Kf8 and 6...g6.

r1b2knr/ppp2pp1/2np4/2bNp2p/2BqP3/3P1Q1N.text:
This is a very tricky move! Black wants to meet c2-c3 with Qxc4 and Bg4. We are still completely winning, but need to proceed with caution.

We move the king once again! This move is a "cold shower" to Black as it simply refutes the whole idea of ...h5.

r1b2knr/ppp2ppp/2np4/2bNp3/2BqP1Q1/3P3N/.text:
Black plays d7-d6 and opens up an attack on our queen.

We simply move the queen to f3 - out of the vision of Black's bishop & still keeping the threat of c2-c3.

r1b2knr/pppp1pp1/2n5/2bNp1Qp/2BqP3/7N/PP.text:
Black moves the queen to the only safe square and attacks the c4 bishop.

We defend the bishop with d2-d3.

r1b2knr/pppp1pp1/2n5/2bNp2p/2B1P1Q1/7N/P.text:
This counterattack is actually Black's only hope of staying in the game.

Our queen was attacked, so we slide it up to g5 - maintaining the attack on Black's queen.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bNp3/2B1P1Q1/8/PPP.text:
Black defends the g7 pawn with the king and simultaneously moves out of the way of Nxc7+. However, Black is not out of the woods whatsoever.

We attack the queen with Nh3!
As it turns out, Black's queen doesn't really have any squares to move to other than d4, where it is going to get into a lot of trouble.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bNp3/2BqP1Q1/7N/PP.text:
Black moves the queen to the only "safe" square and attacks the c4 bishop.

We defend the bishop with d2-d3. Black's queen is suddenly starting to feel quite stuck, and our main threat would be c2-c3, which would trap Black's queen in the center of the board.

r1b2knr/ppppbpp1/2n5/3Np1Qp/2BqP3/3P3N/P.text: Black retreats the bishop and attacks our queen. This move also frees up the c5 square for Black's queen.

r1b2knr/ppppbpp1/2n5/3Np2p/2BqP3/3P2QN/P.text:
We retreat our queen to g3. Now, it is highly unlikely that you will get this position in a game, but it is the critical variation that Black has to play not to be immediately lost. 

White is still better, the position is significantly more pleasant and easier to play for White, but with absolutely perfect play, Black might only be slightly worse.

Black mirrors our move and naturally develops the bishop to c5.

This variation is known as the "Copycat variation" - since Black is mirroring/copying White's moves. 

This variation is extremely common and has been played in over 120 master games and 320,000 games, but it's a mistake because of 4.Qg4!

In this chapter, Black replies with Nc6.

We simply develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

r4knr/ppp2pp1/2np4/2bNp2p/2BqP1b1/3P1Q1N.text: Black develops the bishop and attacks our queen.

r4knr/ppp2pp1/2np4/2bNp2p/2BqP1b1/3P3N/P.text: We simply slide the queen back to f1. Our threat of trapping Black's queen with c2-c3 is now impossible to prevent and White is completely winning.

r4knr/ppp2ppp/2np4/2bNp3/2BqP3/3P1Q1b/PP.text:
Most players will now play ...Bxh3, and we should not rush to recapture on h3.

Instead, we throw in Rf1 and threaten checkmate on f7.

r4knr/ppp2ppp/2npb3/2bNp3/2BqP3/2PP1Q2/P.text: We finally get to play our idea: c2-c3. Black's queen is now trapped and White is completely winning with a major material advantage.

r4knr/ppp2ppp/2npb3/2bNp3/2BqP3/3P1Q2/PP.text: Black retreats the bishop and defends the f7 square.

Black continues naturally with d7-d6, supporting the e-pawn and preparing to develop the light-squared bishop.

We go a2-a4. This move takes some space on the queenside and frees up the a2 square for our bishop.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/1bn3p1/3Np3/2B1P3/5N2/.text:
...Bb6 is inferior, but considerably more common.

We will play c2-c3. This move supports the b4 and d4 squares: One of our plans is to, at some point, take control of the center with a d4 push or to expand on the queenside with a4 + b4.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/2n2qp1/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2.text:
Black defends f7 with the queen and offers a queen trade.

Don't rush to trade queens! We play Nd5 - attacking Black's queen and threatening to fork Black's king and rook with Nxc7+.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/2bNp3/2B1P3/5q2/.text:
Black is pretty much forced to make this capture.

We recapture on f3 with the knight. Black can defend against Nxc7+ in two ways: ...Bb6 & ...Bd6.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1p1p/2nb2p1/3Np3/2B1P3/5N2/.text: This is, objectively, the better option, although it cramps Black's position by blocking in the d-pawn and consequently makes it difficult for Black to develop the light-squared bishop.
We simply castle our king. White is comfortably better here. Black has to somehow solve the problem of developing the c8 bishop, while in the meantime we will build up in the center with c3 + d4.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p1p/2n2np1/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2.text:
Black castles their king before playing d7-d6.

We play d2-d3 and prepare to develop the dark-squared bishop. 7.d3, and the most common response is 7...d6, which loses immediately to Bg5!

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p1p/5np1/2b1p3/2BnP3/2NP1Q.text: Black should play 7...Nd4, not 7...d6. This forces us to respond with Nxd4 as both our queen and the c2 pawn are threatened.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p1p/5np1/2b5/2BpP3/2NP1Q2/.text:
Black recaptures with the e-pawn.
8...Bxd4 runs into 9.Bg5 and White wins a piece.

We develop our bishop to g5 and attack Black's knight. Now capturing on c3 is not a great option since we would capture the f6 knight with our bishop and win full control of the dark squares on the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/ppppbp1p/5np1/1N4B1/2BpP3/3P1Q2.text: We play Nb5 and attack the d4 pawn which really can't be conveniently defended. White has a pleasant advantage in this position.

r1bq1rk1/ppppbp1p/5np1/6B1/2BpP3/2NP1Q2/.text: Therefore, Black should defend the knight with ...Be7.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/2b1p3/2B1P1Q1/2N.text:
4...g6 is the second most common move. By playing g7-g6, Black has successfully defended the g-pawn but has also significantly weakened the dark squares on the kingside. 

We must now notice that our queen on g4 is vulnerable and Black is threatening to win a piece with ...d5.

We will slide the queen back to f3 and line up an attack on the f7 square. Black has two ways to deal with that: 5...Nf6 and 5...Qf6.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black mirrors our move and naturally develops the bishop to c5.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/2np1npp/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP1Q.text: Black can also play ...h6 and prevent us from developing our bishop to g5 or h6.
Instead we develop the bishop to d2 and prepare O-O-O. White now has a pleasant advantage due to the lead in development and Black's weakened kingside.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p1p/2n2np1/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2Q.text:

We proceed by developing our other knight to e2, from where it supports the d4 square and prevents potential ...Nd4 ideas.

Black develops the light-squared bishop and attacks our queen.

We are forced to slide the queen over to g3 as it is the only safe square.

r2qk2r/ppp2p1p/2np1np1/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP2Q.text:
This is the most common move in the lichess database.

Let's recapture.

r2qk2r/ppp2p1p/2np1np1/2b1p3/2B1P3/3P2Q1.text: Play can now develop in a handful of ways. The position is pretty comfortable and our general ideas include Qf3, developing the dark-squared bishop (to g5/h6), c3 and even O-O-O.

r2qk2r/ppp2p1p/2npbnp1/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP2Q.text:
Black retreats the bishop to e6 and offers a trade.

We should trade the bishops on e6 and damage Black's structure.

r2qk2r/ppp4p/2nppnp1/2b1p3/4P3/2NP2Q1/PP.text:
Black recaptures on e6.

We develop our bishop to h6 - using the fact that the dark squares on the king-side were weakened with ...g6.

r3k1nr/ppp2p1p/1bnpb1p1/3Np1N1/P1B1P3/2P.text: We play Ng5 and attack Black's bishop with the intention to capture it. White is now much better on all three parts of the board and Black doesn't really have any good moves. The engines already suggest that White is completely winning with a +2.5 advantage.

r3k1nr/pppq1p1p/2np2p1/2b1p3/2B1P1bQ/2NP.text: Passively retreating the knight to g8 is actually a better option for Black, though White should still be able to obtain a pleasant position.
We develop the bishop to d2 and prepare O-O-O after which play can develop in a couple of different ways. Our general ideas include f3/f4, Nd5 and Bg5.

r3k2r/ppp1q2p/2nppnpB/2b1p3/4P3/2NP2Q1/P.text: Black develops the queen and prepares O-O-O.

r3k2r/ppp1q2p/2nppnpB/2b1p3/N3P3/3P2Q1/P.text: We play Na4 with the intention to, at some point, capture the bishop. The position is quite pleasant; we will castle queenside and play will develop from there.

r3k2r/pppq1p1p/2np1np1/2b1p3/2B1P1b1/2NP.text:
Black develops the queen, supports the g4 bishop and prepares O-O-O.

Qh4 is a neat move! We use the fact that ...Qd7 undefended the f6 knight and immediately try to take advantage of that. Black should then move the knight and has two options: ...Nh5 & ...Ng8.

r3k2r/pppq1p1p/2np2p1/2b1p2n/2B1P1bQ/2NP.text:
Black moves the knight to h5 - this is most common.

Let's play f3. We attack the bishop and force it to move back to e6.

r3k2r/pppq1p1p/2npb1p1/2b1p2n/2B1P1PQ/2N.text: We attack the knight with g2-g4 and Black has a pretty hard time dealing with the attack. White is better here and the engine is already suggesting Black gives up a pawn with Nf4.

r3k2r/pppq1p1p/2npb1p1/2b1p2n/2B1P2Q/2NP.text: Black retreats the bishop to e6.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We will play Nc3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're continuing our analysis of the "Copycat variation" in the Vienna and looking at Black's second most common option on move four: 4...g6.

r1b2knr/pppp1p1p/5p2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.text: We play c2-c3 and prepare to expand in the center with d2-d4. White has a pleasant advantage here due to Black's ruined pawn structure (doubled f-pawns) and the slight lead in development.

r1b2knr/pppp1p1p/5p2/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.text: Black captures our knight with the g-pawn, since capturing with the knight would allow us to capture the e5-pawn.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/1bn5/3Np3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.text: ...Bb6 is the most common way for Black to defend.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/1bn5/3Np3/P1B1P3/5N2/1P.text: We go a2-a4. This move takes some space on the queenside and frees up the a2 square for our bishop. White definitely has a pleasant advantage in this position and our general plan consists of d3 + c3 & even taking more queenside space with b4. Our plan can also consist of O-O, though it is very optional in this case since the king is actually pretty well positioned in the center of the board.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/2n2q2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2Q2.text:
Black defends f7 with the queen and offers a queen trade - but this is actually inaccurate.

Don't rush to trade queens! We play Nd5 - attacking Black's queen and threatening to capture the pawn on c7.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/2n2q2/2bNp3/2B1P3/5Q2/P.text: Don't rush to trade queens! We play Nd5 - attacking Black's queen and threatening to capture the pawn on c7.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bNp3/2B1P3/5q2/PPP.text:
Black captures our queen on f3.

We recapture on f3 with the knight. Black will then defend against Nxc7 in two ways: ...Bb6 & ...Bd6.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/2nb4/3Np3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.text: This is also a decent way for Black to defend the c7-pawn, although it cramps Black's position by blocking in the d-pawn and consequently makes it difficult for them to develop the light-squared bishop.

We simply castle our king. White has a very comfortable position here. Black has to somehow solve the problem of developing the c8 bishop, while in the meantime we will build up in the center with c3 + d4.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/5N2/2b1p3/2B1P3/5n2/PPP.text:
Black captures our queen with check.

We recapture on f3 with the knight.

r1b2knr/pppp1ppp/5q2/2bNp3/2BnP3/5Q2/PPP.text:
Black can also counterattack our queen on f3.

We should capture Black's queen on f6.

r1bq1k1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2Q.text:
Black plays d7-d6, supporting the e-pawn and preparing to develop the light-squared bishop.

We play h2-h3, preventing Black's light-squared bishop from developing to the g4 square...

r1bq1k1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2Q.text:
Black develops the knight and defends against the threat of Qxf7#.

We proceed by developing our knight to e2, from where it supports the d4 square and prevents potential ...Nd4 ideas.

r1bq1knr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P1Q1/2N5/.text:
Black defends the g-pawn with the king - sacrificing the right to castle. This might seem somewhat risky at first glance, but we don't really have a way to immediately expose the king's placement. We must now notice that our queen on g4 is vulnerable and Black is threatening to win a piece with ...d5.

We should play Qf3.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black mirrors our move and naturally develops the bishop to c5.

We now play 4.Qg4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
Black replies with Nc6. 

We will develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

r2q1k1r/ppp2ppp/2npbn2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2Q1.text: So Black develops the bishop to e6.

r2q1k1r/ppp2ppp/2npbn2/2b1p3/4P3/1BN2Q1P.text: We slide the bishop back to b3 - inviting Black to trade on our terms and open the a-file for our rook. White is slightly better in this position and our general plan consists of d2-d3, developing the dark-squared bishop and castling our king.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We will play Nc3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're concluding our analysis of the "Copycat variation" in the Vienna, and looking at Black's third most common, but also most challenging option on move four: 4...Kf8.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/1bP1P3/2N2Q2/P.text: Black plays d7-d6, supporting the e-pawn and preparing to develop the light-squared bishop.

We simply castle our king. White has a minor edge in this position and we will continue to develop with b2-b3, Ng3 & Bg5. Also, most natural for Black is now to attack our queen with ...Bg4 after which we should simply move our queen to d3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/2b1p3/2P1P3/2N2Q2/P.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop before playing d7-d6.

We offer to exchange the dark-squared bishops.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/1bP1P3/2N2Q2/PP.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop before playing d7-d6 and pins our c3 knight.

We continue naturally by developing our knight to e2 and supporting the c3 knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2P1P3/2N1Q3/PPP.text: We recapture with the queen. There is no immediate danger for either side and the development is now pretty flexible. We will continue by developing our knight to e2 (from where it will generally go to g3), solidifying our queenside structure with b2-b3, and freely choosing where to castle our king.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2p2n2/n3p3/2B1P3/2NP1Q.text: We'll respond by developing our knight to e2. There are many ways for Black to approach this position, but our general plan is to develop with h3 + O-O and we can even play on the queenside with a2-a4. Also, we can meet the natural ...b5 with Bb3.
This is the critical continuation - you will pretty much never face this. Black delays capturing on c4 and plays ...c6 - supporting further expansion with ...b5 or ...d5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2P1P3/2N2Q2/P.text:
Black plays d7-d6, supporting the e-pawn and preparing to develop the light-squared bishop.

We play h2-h3, preventing Black's light-squared bishop from developing to the g4 square...

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight naturally on f6 and puts some pressure on our e-pawn.

We play d2-d3.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2n1P3/2NP1Q2/P.text: Black justifies ...Na5 and captures the bishop, and we will recapture, leaving Black with a few plausible options for us to consider.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/n3p3/2B1P3/2NP4/PP.text:
This is the critical move and Black's best attempt at equalizing! You won't face this often but it is important to know how to correctly respond. With ...Na5 Black is quickly exposing the downside of our move d2-d3. When we played d2-d3, we closed our c4 bishop's retreat route, and Black is quickly able to make use of that by attacking the bishop & grabbing the bishop pair.

Let's bring our queen out to f3 to control d5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
In this chapter, Black replies with Nc6. 

We will develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2ppbn2/4p3/2P1P3/1PN2Q1P/.text: Black continues natural development and prevents some Nd5 ideas that we might have in certain positions.

This position can be reached from various move orders (Black can play O-O before c6 or Be7 before Be6 etc.). The setups and general middlegame ideas for White and Black are quite consistent. From an evaluation standpoint, White is slightly better in this position. Black is somewhat cramped, we have a great grip on the d5 square with our c and e pawns and will continue to develop as is highlighted on the board.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/3pbn2/4p3/2P1P3/1PN2Q1P/.text:
Black continues developing naturally.

We develop our knight to the e2 square and prepare O-O.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3pbn2/4p3/2P1P3/2N2Q1P/P.text:
So Black develops the bishop to e6 and attacks our c4-pawn.

We defend the c4-pawn and solidify our queenside pawn structure.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight in order to preserve the f2-f4 push.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this chapter, we're continuing our analysis of 2...Nc6 and looking at the most popular variation of the Vienna - The Three Knights Vienna, characterized by the move 3...Nf6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/4p3/2B1P3/P1NP4.text: Black supports the e-pawn and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/4p3/2B1PP2/P1NP.text: We expand with f2-f4 and prepare a kingside attack. If allowed, we will also play f4-f5 to close the center and the diagonal. White has a comfortable edge in this position.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/b3p3/2B1PP2/P1N.text: Black supports the e-pawn with d7-d6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/b3pP2/2B1P3/P1N.text: This is important! We close the center with f4-f5 and prepare to attack Black on the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/2B5/2PP1Q2/P1P2.text: We develop our queen to f3. White is better and the computer suggests that Black's best attempt is to voluntarily double their e-pawns with Be6. Our attacking ideas are vast - we can expand on the queenside with a2-a4, our bishop can develop to a3 and we can put pressure on Black's e-pawn with Re1.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb4/4p3/P1B5/2PP2N1/2P.text: We expand on the queenside with a4. White has a slight edge and the position is certainly tricky for Black to play. We have various attacking ideas including Ne4, Qf3/Qh5 and Re1.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p1B1/1bB1P3/2NP.text: We develop our bishop to g5 and pin Black's knight. We will place our knight onto the d5 square and quickly attack Black with f2-f4. A natural move like ...h6 can now simply be met with Bxf6 + Nd5. White has a pleasant advantage in this position.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/1bB1P3/2NP4/.text: d7-d6 is most common - Black supports the e-pawn and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/1bn2n1p/4p3/1PB1P3/P1N.text: Black retreats the bishop to b6 - maintaining the pin.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/1bn2n1p/4p3/NPB1P3/P2P.text: We jump our knight out to a4 with the intention to capture Black's bishop - not only will this win us the bishop pair, but it will also finally allow us to play our desired f2-f4. White has easier play and a comfortable advantage.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/2n2n1p/2b1p3/2B1P3/P1N.text:
Black can also move the bishop to c5 - temporarily preventing f2-f4 by pinning our f2 pawn.

We attack the bishop with b2-b4! If the bishop moves off of the g1-a7 diagonal, we will play f2-f4.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/2n2n1p/4p3/1bB1P3/2NP4.text:
...h6 is the other option - Black is preventing us from developing with Bg5.

We attack Black's b4 bishop - forcing a decision. Black has to decide whether to capture on c3 or move the bishop back to a5/c5.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/2n2n1p/4p3/2B1P3/P1bP4.text:
Capturing on c3 is actually the best option.

We recapture on c3 with the knight.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/2n2n1p/b3p3/2B1P3/P1NP.text:
Most common is ...Ba5.

We quickly strike at Black's center with f2-f4!

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/1bB1P3/2NP4/.text:
Black can also O-O and choose to play the position without d7-d5. However, this gives White an edge.

We castle ourselves as well. Black then has two options: ...d6 and ...h6.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp3/1bB1P3/2NP4/P.text:
Black quickly strikes in the center with d7-d5.

We capture the d5-pawn with our e-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np3/1bB5/2NP4/PPP1N.text:
Black recaptures on d5 with the knight.

We castle our king to remove the pin on our knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np3/2B5/2bP4/PPP1NP.text:
Black captures on c3 with the bishop.

We recapture on c3 with the knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/1bB5/2nP4/PPP1NP.text:
Black captures on c3 with the knight.

We recapture with the b-pawn - damaging our structure but gaining an important tempo on Black's bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/2B5/2nP4/PPP2PPP.text:
Black exchanges knights on c3 and damages our queenside pawn structure.

We recapture on c3.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/4p3/2B5/2PP4/P1P1NP.text:
Black retreats the bishop to d6.

We move our knight to g3. From there, it has access to e4 and even f5 in some cases.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/1bB1P3/2NP4/P.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop and pins our c3 knight. The main idea of this move is that Black is trying to "undermine" our central control and quickly strike with d7-d5.

We develop our knight to e2 and support the c3 knight. This move also supports a future f2-f4 and the knight will often go to g3.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight naturally on f6 and puts some pressure on our e-pawn.

We play d2-d3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
In this chapter, Black replies with Nc6. 

We will develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

r2q1r1k/ppp2p1p/5p1B/3b4/3p4/P1NP4/1PP3P.text:
Black moves the king to h8 and defends against the checkmate threat.

We capture Black's light-squared bishop.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2n5/3bp3/5P2/P1NP4/1PP1.text:
Instead, Black ignores f4 and castles their king.

We push f4-f5 - closing the center and preparing a kingside attack.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/8/3bpP2/3n4/P1NP4/1PP1N.text:
Black puts their knight on d4 and offers an exchange with the intention to simplify the position. This position has been reached in three master games, but we have a very interesting novelty prepared...

f6! This move might seem completely absurd at first but it has a concrete idea - we want to open up Black's king.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p1p/5p2/3b4/3p4/P1NP4/1PP3PP.text:
Black recaptures on d4.

We should not rush to give a check with our queen, but instead we should play Bh6 first. We are attacking Black's rook and threatening checkmate in 2 moves with Qg4+ & Qg7#.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p1p/5p2/3bp3/3n4/P1NP4/1PP1N.text:
Black recaptures with the g-pawn as to not lose material.

We capture the d4 knight and simultaneously open the d1-h5 diagonal for our queen.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/3np3/2B5/P1PP4/2P1.text: Black continues natural development with O-O.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/3np3/P1B5/2PP4/2P1.text: We expand on the queenside with a3-a4. If possible, we would also like to push the pawn to a5. We have two bishops and an open b-file so we can  try to use it. Our dark-squared bishop can develop flexibly (b2/d2/a3). The position is objectively still equal though.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5b2/3bp3/3n4/P1NP4/1PP1N.text:
Black recaptures on f6 with the bishop.

We now play Rxf6! A brilliant exchange sacrifice! We are practically forcing Black to capture with the g-pawn and open their king since Qxf6 would allow us to capture the d5 bishop.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2n1b3/3np3/2B5/P1NP4/1PP.text:
Black decides not to give up the bishop on c3 and instead retreats it to e7.

We capture on d5 with the bishop.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2n5/3bp3/8/P1NP4/1PP1NPP.text:
Black recaptures on d5.

We strike with f2-f4. Black definitely shouldn't capture on f4 since Nxf4 (followed by capturing the light-squared bishop) would be devastating.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/3np3/1bB5/2NP4/PPP1.text:
Black develops with the c8 bishop to e6 and defends the d5 knight.

We attack Black's b4 bishop - forcing a decision. Black now has to decide whether to capture on c3 or retreat the bishop.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/3np3/2B5/P1bP4/1PP1.text:
Black decides to capture on c3 - this is most common.

We are actually forced to recapture with the b-pawn since capturing with the knight would lead to a tripling of the c-pawns.

r4r1k/ppp2p1p/5p1B/3q4/3p4/P2P4/1PP3PP/R.text: We move our queen to f1 and threaten checkmate with Qxf6+ & Qg7#. Black must defend against the threat of checkmate, after which we will capture the f8 rook and enter an objectively equal endgame. Down a pawn for the moment, but with Black's ruined structure and weak king, White should have good compensation.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight in order to preserve the f2-f4 push.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're continuing our analysis of the Three Knights Vienna and looking at Black's second most common choice on move 4: 4...Bb4.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/2B1PP2/2NP4.text:
Black supports the e-pawn and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

We continue with our plan and develop the g1 knight to f3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP4/.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop naturally on the c5 square. This is the most common move, and it allows us to get our desired setup.

We expand with f2-f4 and look to develop our knight behind the f-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight naturally on f6 and puts some pressure on our e-pawn.

We play d2-d3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
In this chapter, Black replies with Nc6.

We will develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2p1p3/2B1PPb1/3P1N.text:
Black recaptures. ...Nd4 is an idea.

But we can just castle.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/N1B1PPb1/3P.text:
Black could simply castle, ignoring the attack on their bishop. 

Their idea is that they'll recapture with the c-pawn and gain a semi-open d-file.

As always, we'll execute our knight for bishop trade because we want to clear the way for 0-0.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2p1p3/2B1PP2/2PP1P1b.text: The bishop attacks our rook, and we remove it from danger.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2p1p3/2B1PPb1/2PP1n2.text: If Black takes, we can recapture.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2p1p3/2BnPPb1/3P1N2/.text:
The idea is that after ...Nd4, we can kick that knight out.

c3 attacks the knight.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2p5/2B1Pp2/2PP1P1b/P.text:
And if Black persists by continuing to go for exchanges, we capture the pawn on f4 back. 

Our center is quite overwhelming.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/8/2p4n/2B1PB2/2PP1P1b/PP.text: If your bishop is attacked, e3 is the best square for it.

r2qk2r/p1p2ppp/3p1n2/b3p3/N1pPPP2/3P3P/P.text: We capture the knight on d4. White is better here. We're castled and ready to shred open the center - Black can't even castle and try to safeguard their king since we would just capture the e-pawn and establish a dominant pawn center.

r2qk2r/p1p2ppp/3p1n2/bp2p3/N1BnPP2/2PP3P.text:
Black forks our a4 knight and c4 bishop with b7-b5.

We unpin our c-pawn by castling the king and are now ready to capture Black's d4 knight.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/1b1p1n2/4p3/N1BnPP2/3P1Q1.text:
Black jumps the knight to d4 - attacking our queen & the c2-pawn.

We retreat the queen to f2 - defending the c-pawn. It might feel counterintuitive to put the queen in direct line of a potential discovered attack from the b6 bishop, but Black simply doesn't have any useful discoveries, and our intention is to capture that bishop on the next move.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/4p3/N1B1PP2/3P1b1.text:
By far most common and most logical is ...Bxf3. Black gives up the bishop pair which was going to be lost anyway and instead gains control over the d4 square.

We don't want to ruin our structure with doubled f-pawns so we recapture on f3 with the queen.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/4p3/N1B1PPb1/3P1N.text:
Black shouldn't allow us to capture on c5 and irreparably damage their pawn structure, so their best option is to retreat the bishop to b6.

We shouldn't rush to capture on b6 - the bishop isn't going anywhere. Instead, we throw in h2-h3 and force a decision from Black's light-squared bishop.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/2B1PPb1/2NP1.text:
Most common is ...Bg4. Black develops the bishop and pins our f3 knight - reducing our control over the d4 square.

Keep Na4 in mind! This is our best way of dealing with ...Bg4 and the threat of ...Nd4. Our move Na4 attacks Black's strong dark-squared bishop and frees up the c3 square so that we can prevent/meet Nd4 with c2-c3.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/2b1p3/N1B1PPb1/2PP1.text: We recapture with the f-pawn - gaining a tempo on Black's light-squared bishop. Black has to move the bishop and we will follow up by capturing the dark-squared bishop on c5 - completely ruining Black's pawn structure.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/2b1p3/N1BnPPb1/3P1N.text:
Black can also try to play ...Nd4 immediately, but this isn't considered to be any good.

We attack the knight with c2-c3.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/b3p3/N1BnPP2/3P3P/P.text: Black's only attempt at saving the bishop is to give a check on a5. The line that follows is very forced: we block the check with c2-c3.

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/8/2p4n/2B1P2q/2PPBP1b/PP1Q.text: We've got strong ideas of Bxc5, Kh1, and the engine's best move for Black is the unintuitive ...Be6!

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/8/2p4n/2B1P2q/2PPBP1b/PP3R.text: If the queen comes into h4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight in order to preserve the f2-f4 push.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're continuing our analysis of the Three Knights Vienna and looking at Black's most common choice on move 4: 4...Bc5.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/3p1q1p/n1b1pP2/2B1P1P1/3.text: We start a kingside attack with g2-g4! Our general plan is now to continue with Qe2 + Be3 + O-O-O and even a well-timed g4-g5. White has a very pleasant position and a brewing attack which is, practically, very difficult to defend against.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/3p1q1p/n1b1pP2/2B1P3/3P1.text: Black recaptures with the queen to keep the kingside pawn structure intact.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/4pP1R/2B1Pq2/2NP4/P.text: Black moves the queen to f4 and gives a check.

Make sure to move the king to g1 - we don't really want to be offering any queen trades with moves like Qf3, since we are currently down a pawn.  According to the computer, White has a winning advantage, but this advantage can be tricky to prove in practical play.

The computer evaluates this position as +2.5 for White, but in Frank, Mario Alberto - Krol, Wladyslaw (2001.), White didn't manage to convert his advantage and the game ended in a draw.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/4pPq1/2B1P3/2NP4/PP.text:
Black grabs the pawn on g5.

We move the rook to h5 and attack Black's queen.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp1n2/2b1pPB1/2P1P3/2N2.text: We develop the queen to e2 and prepare O-O-O. We have a pleasant advantage and our game plan is to attack Black on the kingside with our g and h pawns. Most games now continue h6 Bxf6, after which we will be able to combine O-O-O, g2-g4 and h2-h4 to start a crushing attack on Black's kingside.
This is by far the most common idea. Black plays c7-c6 and covers the d5 square with the c-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp1n2/2b1pPB1/2P1P3/P1N.text: We recapture on c4 and will continue to develop with Qe2 and O-O-O. The reason that this move order is actually a better option for Black is simply because we got the same position as in the main continuation, just that we used an extra tempo on a2-a3. This means all of our typical ideas will come a move "slower" and Black has a little bit more time to try to consolidate. However, our position is still much easier to play and we have a comfortable objective edge.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp1n2/2b1pPB1/2n1P3/P1N.text: Black captures on c4 as to not allow us to keep the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp1n2/n1b1pPB1/2B1P3/2N.text:
Black can also continue ...c6 immediately - this is slightly more accurate and I will explain why at the end of the line.

We play a2-a3, threatening to "save" our light-squared bishop by retreating it to a2.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp4/2b1pP2/4P3/1P1P1N2/.text: We recapture with the a-pawn. The position is very rich & dynamic and, objectively, White has a slight edge. We will develop our queen to e2 and our dark-squared bishop can develop to d2 or offer to trade itself on e3. We also have great attacking potential with g2-g4 and h2-h4.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp4/2b1pP2/4P3/1n1P1N2/.text: Black captures the bishop on b3.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pp4/2bBpP2/3nP3/3P1N2/P.text:
Black attacks our bishop with c7-c6.

We retreat the bishop to b3, allowing Black to capture our bishop and grab the bishop pair.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/2b1pP2/2B1P3/2N.text:
Black can also play prophylactically by preventing Bg5 with h7-h6.

We will continue with Nd5, offering a trade of knights.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np3p/2bBpP2/4P3/3P1N2/.text: We recapture on d5. White has a comfortable advantage and our general development plan is now Qe2 + Bd2 + O-O-O. Any attack on our bishop can comfortably be met with Bb3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np3p/2bnpP2/2B1P3/3P1N.text: Black captures our knight on d5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/3p1n1p/n1bNpP2/2B1P3/3P.text:
Black can also decline the trade and continue by attacking our bishop with ...Na5.

We capture the knight on f6 with check.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/2B1PP2/2NP.text:
...O-O is second most common behind ...Bg4. Black doesn't initiate any immediate battles and instead quickly safeguards the king.

f5 is a common idea in these positions.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1pPN1/2B1P3/2N.text: ...Nf6 is not the most common, but is the most resilient.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2bNpPN1/2B1P3/3P.text:
We put our knight on d5 with the intention to trade it off on f6, after which we will continue our attack with g4 and h4. 

White has a lot of easy play and a very pleasant advantage.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b1p1N1/2B1PPn1/2N.text:
By far most common is ...O-O - safeguarding the king and keeping the threat of Nf2 alive.

We continue f4-f5! We've now closed the h3-c8 diagonal and are threatening to capture Black's undefended g4 knight.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b1pPN1/2B1P3/2NP4.text: This is the most common move, but a massive blunder!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b1pPNQ/2B1P3/2NP4.text: We play Qh5! Black cannot defend against the threats on the f7 & h7 pawns. White is now completely winning - the computer is even suggesting that Black is so lost, that their best option is to give up the queen with ...Qxg5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/4pPN1/2B1P1n1/2NP4.text:
Black can also give this check on f2 and force some exchanges. This move is about as common as ...Nf6.

We move the king to f1.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/4pPN1/2B1P3/2NPb3/.text:
Black recaptures on e3 and attacks our knight.

We defend the knight with h2-h4! This move is handy since we will also be able to open the h-file for our rook upon recapturing.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/4pPN1/2B1P3/2NPn3/.text:
Black plays Ne3+ - forking our king & queen.

We are forced to capture the knight since we don't want to lose our queen.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/4pPb1/2B1P2P/2NP4/.text:
Black captures the knight on g5.

We recapture on g5 and open the h- file. The g-pawn is now en prise.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/2b1pP2/2BnP3/2NP1.text:
This is a close second in popularity to the main move ...Na5.

We don't simply capture on d4, but instead respond with Nd5!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/2b1pPB1/2n1P3/2NP.text:
Black justifies ...Na5 and captures the bishop.

We recapture on c4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4pPB1/1bP1P3/2N2N.text:
This is critical, but considerably rarer than ...c6. Black pins the c3 knight, thereby preventing Nd5.

Nd2! We can now play this completely absurd computer suggested novelty! We allow Black to triple our c-pawns, but quickly begin a three move reroute of the f3 knight, which wasn't really playing a major role.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4pPB1/2P1P3/2P5/P.text: We recapture on c3. Our main idea is now to reroute the knight through f1 to e3 or g3. Black is cramped and has troubles getting their other pieces into play, while we still have the standard attacking ideas with g2-g4 and h2-h4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4pPB1/2P1P3/2b5/P.text: Black captures on c3 and forces us to triple the c-pawns.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/n1b1pP2/2B1P3/2NP.text:
...Na5 is the most common move. Black attacks the c4 bishop and tries to quickly grab the bishop pair.

We ignore Black's threat and pin the f6 knight. In a perfect world, we will place our knight on the d5 square and capture Black's f6 knight - completely ruining Black's kingside pawn structure.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p4/2bnpP2/2BnP3/3P1N2/.text:
Black captures our knight on d5.

We recapture on d5.

r1bq4/pppk2p1/3p1p2/2b1pPP1/2B1P3/2NP3Q/.text: Black runs the king to d7!

r1bq4/pppk2pQ/3p1p2/2b1pPP1/2B1P3/2NP4/P.text: We move our queen to h7 and attack the g-pawn. Black is incredibly underdeveloped and will simply not be able to deal with our attack. White is completely winning.

r1bqk2r/ppp2B1p/2np2p1/2b1p1NQ/4PP2/2NP4.text: We throw in Bxf7+! Black's king is now forced to move and simply won't be able to survive the oncoming attack.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p1p/2np2p1/2b1p1NQ/2B1PP2/2N.text: Black defends against the mate threat by moving the g-pawn and attacking our queen.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2np3p/2b1p1N1/2B1PPn1/2N.text:
Black attacks our knight with h7-h6. This move might not make much sense at first glance, but we actually shouldn't rush to capture the f7-pawn, since it would allow an annoying Qh4+.

Instead, we should continue f4-f5.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2np4/2b1pPp1/2B1P1n1/2NP.text:
Black captures the knight on g5.

We capture Black's knight on g4.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p3/2B1PP2/2NP4.text:
Black supports the e-pawn and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

We continue with our plan and develop the g1 knight to f3.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b1p1N1/2B1PP2/2NP4.text:
The immediate ...Nf2 might look attractive, but it is a massive mistake!

We play Qh5! - threatening checkmate on f7.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b1p3/2B1PPn1/2NP1N.text:
Black jumps the knight to g4 and threatens a fork on f2. At first glance, it might seem as though White doesn't really have a good defense against the threat of Nf2, but unbeknownst to Black, we have a really nice response prepared.

We counterattack Black's f7 pawn with Ng5!

r1bqk2r/ppp3p1/2np1p2/2b1pPp1/2B1P1Q1/2N.text:
Black solidifies the kingside pawn structure and supports the g-pawn with f7-f6.

We play h2-h4. In a perfect world, we will be able to open the h-file and quickly get to Black's king.

r1bqk2r/ppp3p1/3p1p2/2b1pPp1/2B1P1QP/2NP.text:
Black captures the a1 rook.

We capture on g5 and open the h-file. This is where Black's issues become apparent.

Black continues with their plan and plays Nxc2+.

We move the king to d1 and attack Black's knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp3p1/3p1p2/2b1pPp1/2BnP1QP/2NP.text:
Black jumps the knight into d4 and threatens Nxc2+, forking our king and rook. However, Black is certainly not ready for our next move.

We completely ignore Black's threat and play Rh3! The idea is that the rook on h3 is defended by the queen, and we want to shred open the h-file to get to Black's king.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP4/.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop naturally on the c5 square. This is most common and allows us to get our desired set-up.

We expand with f2-f4 and look to develop our knight behind the f-pawn.

r1bqk3/ppp3p1/3p1p2/2b1pPP1/2B1P1Q1/2NP3.text:
Black captures our rook on h3.

We recapture on h3 with the queen. The devastating threat is now Qh8+.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight naturally on f6 and puts some pressure on our e-pawn.

We play d2-d3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
In this chapter, Black replies with Nc6. 

We will develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight in order to preserve the f2-f4 push.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're continuing our analysis of the Three Knights Vienna and looking at Black's most common choice on move 4: 4...Bc5, with deviations on move 6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/8/2BPPB2/2N2N2/.text:
Black retreats the bishop to b6, keeping pressure on our d-pawn which can quickly come under fire.

We continue with Bg5. Black was actually threatening a typical tactical idea with ...Nxe4 Nxe4 d5!, so we opt to pin the f6 knight in order to prevent said idea.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b5/2B1PB2/2NP1N.text:
Black continues naturally and safeguards the king with O-O.

We play d3-d4! This move is pretty rare, but it is the top choice of the engine.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/6B1/1bBPP3/2N2N2.text: We respond with Bg5, pinning Black's knight! Our development plan is now O-O + Qd3. We will also capture Black's knight when our g5 bishop is provoked with a move like h7-h6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/8/1bBPPB2/2N2N2/.text: Black responds Bb4, pinning our c3 knight and thereby threatening to capture the e-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1PP2/2NP.text:
Black immediately safeguards the king with O-O.

We continue with our plan and develop the g1 knight to f3.  Now the main moves 6...d6 and 6...exf4 transpose.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1PPn1/2NP1.text:
...Ng4! Black is eyeing the f2 square with their pieces and our typical response Ng5 isn't as effective since Black has already castled and is now ready to meet Ng5 with d7-d5!

Instead we simply move our queen and avoid the knight fork on f2. If ...Nf2, we play Rf1.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1PPn1/2NP1N2.text:
Instead, Black plays Bf2+ and forces our king to move.

We slide the king over to f1.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BbPP2/2NP3P/PPP.text: Black continues with Nf2 and attacks our rook.
We move the rook to g1. Ideally, we want to continue by trading Black's bishop with Be3. This position is still objectively equal, but Black's only good move is the pawn sacrifice with d7-d5.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BbPPn1/2NP4/PPP.text:
Black recaptures on d4 with their bishop.

We continue h2-h3 and force Black's knight to move.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BnPPn1/2NP1N2/P.text:
Black jumps their other knight into d4 and attacks our queen.

We capture the d4 knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b5/2B1PB2/2NP4/P.text:
Black plays d7-d6, preparing to develop the light-squared bishop.

Let's play Nf3 to develop.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP4/.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop naturally on the c5 square. This is most common and allows us to get our desired set-up.

We expand with f2-f4 and look to develop our knight behind the f-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2B1Pp2/2NP4/P.text:
Black captures the f4-pawn. It might seem as though this move only helps us develop, but Black actually has some very concrete ideas.

We recapture on f4 and develop our c1 bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight naturally on f6 and puts some pressure on our e-pawn.

We play d2-d3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
In this chapter, Black replies with Nc6. 

We will develop the light-squared bishop to c4. In a perfect world, we'll play d3, f4, Nf3, and castle.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1b1p1n2/6B1/2BnP3/2N2P2/.text:
Black captures the d-pawn.

We slide our queen over to g2 and are ready to start a kingside attack.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1b1pnn2/6B1/2B1P2P/2N2P2.text: We support the bishop with h2-h4. Black now shouldn't capture the g5 bishop as the opening of the h-file would lead to a crushing attack. Down a pawn for the moment, but with rich attacking ideas and great dynamic compensation. The position is objectively equal, but requires very accurate defense from Black.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1b1pnn2/6B1/2B1P3/2N2P2/.text: Black retreats the knight to e6 and attacks our g5 bishop.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/6B1/2BPP1b1/2N2N.text:
Black develops the light-squared bishop and pins our f3-knight. Black's main idea is to capture the knight and win the d-pawn.

We continue Qd2 - preparing to castle queenside.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/6B1/2BPP3/2N2b2/.text:
Black continues with their plan and captures on f3.

We recapture on f3.

r2qk2r/1pp2ppp/p1npbn2/1Bb5/4PB2/2NP1N2/.text:
Black attacks our bishop and forces a decision.

We continue with our plan by capturing on c6 and ruining Black's pawn structure.

r2qk2r/2p2ppp/p1ppbn2/2b5/4PB2/2NP1N2/PP.text: We continue Qd2 and prepare O-O-O. White has a slight advantage and we will continue to develop with O-O-O + Rhe1. The middlegame ideas are rich, but one of our main game plans is to play in the center by preparing an eventual e4-e5 or d3-d4.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b5/2B1PBb1/2NP1N2.text: Black develops the light-squared bishop and pins our f3 knight.

We simply move out of the pin and prepare O-O-O. The position is pretty comfortable and some typical middlegame ideas include Bg5 and Nd5. In many variations, one of our rooks will also move to the f-file in order to meet an eventual ...Nd4 from Black.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2npbn2/2b5/2B1PB2/2NP1N2/.text:
Black develops the light-squared bishop to e6 and offers a trade.

We decline the trade and move the bishop to b5. We want to ruin Black's structure by capturing on c6, and develop with Qd2 + O-O-O.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the mirror image e5, the most popular reply at all levels.

We develop our queenside knight in order to preserve the f2-f4 push.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we're concluding our analysis of the Three Knights Vienna and looking at Black's most common choice on move 4: 4...Bc5, with earlier deviations on move 5.
